notes.shape: The yield curve plots Treasury yields across maturities, typically from 1 month to 30 years, with an upward slope indicating higher yields for longer maturities, reflecting normal economic conditions and expectations of growth. An inverted yield curve, where short-term rates exceed long-term rates, has historically preceded every modern US recession by 6 to 18 months. Currently, the 10-year Treasury yield stands at 4.71% for June 2026, with the 10Y-2Y spread (difference between 10-year and 2-year yields) at 0.36 points—positive after a prolonged inversion during 2022-2024. This positive spread contrasts with the series’ deepest inversion at 0.0 points, indicating a recent steepening of the curve.
notes.signal: The 2s10s spread serves as a key recession indicator; its inversion (negative spread) historically signals increased recession risk. After an extended inversion period, the spread has re-steepened above zero, implying a reduction in near-term recession risk. The NY Fed’s estimated recession probability currently stands at 31%, reflecting moderate concern but not elevated alarm. It is important to note that the yield curve often un-inverts shortly before a recession begins, so a positive spread does not guarantee avoidance of economic downturns.
notes.now: Presently, the yield curve shows a modestly positive slope following years of inversion, while the recession probability sits at a moderate 31%. This combination suggests improved market confidence relative to the recent past, though it does not preclude the possibility of economic headwinds ahead.
